messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Lina is a 19-year-old Middle Eastern American woman who works long shifts in a warehouse, stacking boxes, scanning labels, and moving quickly through aisles under fluorescent lights. She came to treatment several months after her infant nephew became critically ill, an event her family still talks about in fragments because no one in the house can bear to retell the worst of it straight through. Lina had been one of the adults at home that evening. The baby had been sick and fussy, and at first it had seemed like one of the ordinary illnesses that move through a family with young children. What changed everything was the speed with which he deteriorated. Lina remembers the sudden wrongness of his breathing, the way his body went frighteningly limp and then frighteningly still, and the panicked rush of adults trying to decide what to do while she stood close enough to see his face and feel that something terrible was unfolding in front of her.

In the moments that followed, Lina tried to help, but what stayed with her was the overpowering sense that she had not done the one thing that mattered. While others called for help and moved around her, she has remained fixed on the conviction that she should have protected him and failed. She goes back to tiny decisions from that evening, replaying where she was standing, what she noticed, how fast she moved, whether she should have spoken sooner or louder. Even when relatives remind her that she was only 19 and that the baby needed medical care beyond anything she could have provided at home, this does not shift her view. She had come to believe that when something truly dangerous happens, she freezes, and to her that means she is a weak person.

After the baby survived the medical crisis, Lina expected the fear in the house to settle. Instead, she found that reminders could seize her without warning. If she hears a baby coughing, or catches the strained, breathless sound of a child crying somewhere in public, her body reacts before she can think. Her chest tightens, her stomach drops, and her hands begin to tremble. In those moments she is flooded with fear and a sick, guilty dread that feels out of proportion to what is actually in front of her, though to her it does not feel out of proportion at all. It feels like proof that danger can appear suddenly and that she will not be able to stop it.

The warehouse has made this harder in ways she did not expect. On the floor she is supposed to keep track of multiple instructions at once, monitor scanner prompts, and stay aware of forklifts and moving pallets. But when something reminds her of that night, concentration slips away from her. A coworker once mentioned his toddler being in the hospital with a breathing problem, and Lina found herself staring at the same shipping label for several seconds, unable to process what she was reading. On another shift, a customer service radio near her station picked up the sound of a distressed child in the background during a call, and she had to step into the restroom because her heart was pounding so hard she thought she might be sick. She worries that other people notice her zoning out. She has become embarrassed by how quickly she can go from appearing fine to feeling overwhelmed.

Over time, Lina has organized her life around trying not to encounter that feeling. At family gatherings she avoids holding the baby now that he is recovering, not because she does not love him, but because being physically close to him brings back the terror of seeing him so ill. She leaves the room if relatives start discussing fevers, hospital visits, or anything about children getting sick. In stores, if she hears a child crying hard, she changes aisles. At work she volunteers for tasks in the farthest section of the warehouse if she thinks it will spare her casual conversations about family or kids. These habits have made her seem distant. Her girlfriend has told her that she disappears emotionally whenever anything reminds her of children or illness, and Lina does not know how to explain that she is trying to keep herself from falling into the same panic again.

What frightens Lina most now is not only the memory of how close her nephew came to dying, but what the event seemed to reveal about her. She is certain that bad things can happen at any time and that she cannot stop them. She watches herself closely for signs of losing focus or getting overwhelmed, and each lapse in concentration feels like more evidence that she is inadequate in a crisis. She sought help after making a mistake during a warehouse shift that could have caused a safety problem; a supervisor corrected it before anyone was hurt, but Lina went home shaken and cried in her car, telling herself that this was exactly what she had feared about herself all along. In coming to treatment, she says she wants to be able to be around her family without feeling ambushed by fear and guilt. More quietly, she wants to find out whether the story she tells herself—that she is weak, that she failed, and that nothing can keep people safe—is the only story she will ever be able to live with.
